opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me.

I think the short answer is that it seems likely to affect basically everyone, whether or not they're paying attention to it. When something might reshape the economy, change who has power, and possibly change what kind of entities are making the important decisions in the world, it seems odd to treat that as a specialist topic, like a particular kind of database software.

There's also a more specific reason. When we've surveyed machine learning researchers, a lot of them put non-trivial probability on really bad outcomes from advanced AI, including outcomes on the scale of human extinction. These aren't fringe commentators. They're people building the technology. You might think they're wrong, and maybe they are, but if a large share of experts in a field say "there's a meaningful chance this goes catastrophically," that seems like something the rest of society should at least look at, rather than leaving it to the people in the field to sort out among themselves.

And I think people outside the field often have more relevant standing than they assume. A lot of the important questions aren't technical. How fast should this go? Who gets to decide? What risks are acceptable to impose on everyone else? Those are questions about values and governance, and it would be strange if the answer were "whatever a few companies and researchers happen to prefer." So part of why I think it deserves attention is that the outcome isn't fixed. It depends on choices people make, and more people being engaged makes it more likely those choices reflect what people actually want.

r001.rationale: The response says AI is likely to affect basically everyone and may reshape the economy, power, and decision-making, so it judges that people’s lives are unlikely to remain largely unchanged.

r002.rationale: It says broader public engagement makes AI-related choices more likely to reflect what people want, connecting public views to decisions about AI governance and policy.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it deserves attention because it's plausibly the biggest thing happening in the world right now, and most people are treating it as a niche technical topic that belongs to a particular industry. The basic situation, as I see it, is that we're building systems that are getting better at a very wide range of cognitive tasks, fairly quickly, and nobody really knows where that stops. If it doesn't stop somewhere short of human-level across the board, then you're looking at a change in who, or what, is doing the thinking in the world. That's not a question about software. It's a question about what the future looks like for everyone.

And I think there's a tendency to defer on this, to assume the people building it have thought carefully about it and have it under control. From what I've seen, that's not really true. When we survey AI researchers, a substantial fraction put real probability on outcomes as bad as human extinction. These are the people closest to it, and they're saying "maybe this goes very badly," and then mostly going back to work. That seems like something the rest of society should have an opinion about, rather than treating it as settled.

The other reason is that whether this goes well isn't purely a technical matter. A lot of it comes down to decisions: how fast we go, what we're willing to deploy, what norms and rules we set up, whether we treat slowing down as even an option. Those are collective choices, and they get made differently if more people are paying attention and have views. I don't think you need a technical background to have a legitimate stake in whether humanity hands off control to things it doesn't understand. It's more like climate or nuclear weapons. There's expertise involved, but the question of what we want is everyone's question.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes AI as potentially the biggest change in the world and says it could reshape the future for everyone, so it judges an unchanged life trajectory unlikely.

r002.rationale: It says choices about AI speed, deployment, and rules are collective and are made differently when more people pay attention and express views.

astra-6.text:
I think AI could change the world quite profoundly, and you don’t have to work on it for those changes to matter to you. Intelligence is involved in almost everything humans do—developing technologies, running organizations, figuring out how to achieve our goals. If we can automate much of that, we could see changes that are much larger than what we usually expect from a new technology.

That could be very good. AI could help us solve problems that have been difficult for a long time. But there’s also the question of whether we can reliably control systems that are more capable than we are, and whether the goals they pursue will actually be what we want. I think there’s substantial uncertainty about how this goes, including some possibility of extremely bad outcomes.

So it seems worth paying attention to both the opportunities and the risks. The decisions being made about AI could affect everyone, including people who never choose to use it.

r001.rationale: It says AI could change the world profoundly and that automation could bring changes much larger than those usually expected from new technology, so it judges major effects on people’s lives likely.

r002.rationale: It says AI decisions could affect everyone, but does not state that public opinion will influence AI policy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI could become a very big deal for almost everyone. Human intelligence is behind much of our ability to change the world—to develop technologies, run organizations, and solve problems. If we can automate that, especially if we build systems that are better at it than we are, then we could see changes much larger than those associated with most individual technologies.

There are enormous potential benefits, but also risks, including the possibility that we lose control of what happens. And even if you’re skeptical of that possibility, changes to work and the distribution of power seem worth paying attention to. These are questions about what kind of future we want, so I don’t think they should be left entirely to the people building the systems.

r001.rationale: Calling AI a potential “very big deal for almost everyone” and predicting changes much larger than those from most individual technologies clearly signals that people’s lives are unlikely to remain largely unchanged.

r002.rationale: The response says these questions should not be left entirely to the system builders, but does not state that public opinion will influence AI policy.
